headline: Susan Smith denied parole 32 years after drowning sons in S.C. lake
author: Brady Dennis

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Critic covering digital arts and entertainment
What I saw playing 170 hours of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ before everyone else

Playing “Grand Theft Auto VI” three weeks early felt like I’d shown up too early for the biggest concert festival in human history. Like SZA, the Weeknd and Travis Scott had new music, but I was required by a nondisclosure agreement to not even whisper it to another soul.

Since “GTA VI” was unveiled in 2023, people have been making whole essays about of a few minutes of footage. The game was impossibly beautiful and realistic. It looked like the future. But since late last month, I felt like I was living in that future. I had all the answers of how the game works and all the shocking plot twists throughout its 50- to 100-hour storyline to write my review where I called it the most extraordinary game I’ve ever reviewed.

I wondered what it must’ve felt like to see the “Star Wars: A New Hope” before anyone in 1977 saw it. There must have been a moment where you realized film could do something beyond the limits of imagination at the time. I wondered how long you could sit with that.
On Wednesday, as the game finally released worldwide, I spent hours watching streamers play the opening of “GTA VI.” Even after the 170 hours I spent in the game, I saw things I’d never seen.

I’d been waiting three weeks to tell people what I saw — and now the rest of the world is showing up for the same thing, a rare flash of modern monoculture. I can finally turn to the person in the next seat and ask, “Did you see that?”
National correspondent covering the Southeast
Officials on Thursday unanimously denied parole to Susan Smith, who was convicted of killing her two young sons in 1994 by strapping them into her car and rolling it into a South Carolina lake.
The case gripped the nation at the time, after Smith’s false claim that a Black man had abducted 3-year-old Michael and 14-month-old Alex. She later confessed to drowning them.

“I’m not the same person I was 32 years ago. I have changed. I have grown up. I have matured,” Smith, who was first denied parole in 2024, told the board Thursday. Now 55, she said she carries deep remorse over the “unbearable pain” she caused.
The boys’ father, David Smith, was among a litany of people who pleaded for her to remain behind bars.

“It’s been 32 years since I buried Michael and Alex,” he said, wearing a picture of his sons on the lapel of his suit and fighting back tears. “I know for some of you 32 years is a long time, but for me it was yesterday.”
Setting her free, he said, “would be a huge injustice.”
On Thursday, members of the parole board agreed, by a 6-0 vote.
Reporter covering the business, culture and politics of sports
A ticket to the NWSL final? Be ready to pony up.

Saturday’s NWSL Championship between the Washington Spirit and the Kansas City Current at D.C.’s Audi Field is set to be the most expensive ever. It’s the latest example of an explosion in playoff ticket prices in women’s sports.

According to TickPick, a ticket resale platform, the average ticket has sold for $318, a 212 percent increase from last year’s $102 average for the final, in which Gotham FC beat the Spirit. It also tops the $307 average ticket for the 2025 MLS Cup Final, which Inter Miami CF won over Vancouver Whitecaps FC.

And the prices have only increased since the matchup, which features American stars Trinity Rodman and Croix Bethune, was set on Sunday. As of Wednesday evening, the cheapest ticket cost $328. A fan could have attended all 15 regular season Spirit home games at Audi Field for a combined $312.
Reporter covering the U.S. House of Representatives
Absent Republicans are a problem for House leaders in the lame-duck session
House Republican leaders have a pretty packed to-do list during this lame-duck period.
They have 13 legislative days left.
They also have an attendance problem. Fourteen members missed votes on Wednesday. On Thursday morning, votes trickled in slowly. Twenty-one Republicans didn’t vote.
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) recognized that this is a challenge.

“Attendance is a great frustration for me right now. We’ll be addressing that with members,” he told reporters Thursday morning. “It’s not possible for us to … advance our legislative agenda unless the members are here doing their job.”
Many of the missing lawmakers lost in this month’s midterm elections, and their tenures in Congress will end in early January.
Johnson said he’ll be having individual meetings with members to address the issue “because we have important weeks ahead of us.”
Congress is seeking to stave off a government shutdown (funding ends on Dec. 11), and lawmakers want to pass a major defense policy in coming weeks.
House Republicans also want to push through a spending bill answering President Donald Trump’s demand for $350 billion in funds for the Pentagon to address the ongoing war in Iran.
Reporter covering Florida
Extreme flooding sets records in Florida, with more rain to come
Parts of Florida remained underwater Thursday, with schools closed, residents stranded and little relief in sight as forecasters warned of more downpours.

Along the Space Coast, the National Weather Service warned of life-threatening flash flooding in central Brevard County as bands of heavy rain continued to move ashore. Videos showed cars stranded in floodwaters and neighborhoods submerged. In Palm Bay, emergency crews used boats to evacuate residents.
After days of heavy rain, the St. Johns River, Florida’s longest river, rose to a record 18.1 feet at a gauge west of Cocoa on Thursday morning.

Farther south, Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Broward County had recorded nearly 17 inches of rain over two days by Thursday morning, according to preliminary National Weather Service totals.
The flooding kept public schools in Broward, Miami-Dade and Brevard counties closed Thursday.
A flood watch remained in effect for parts of southeast Florida through Thursday evening, while most of east-central Florida was under a watch through Friday evening.

Forecasters warned that some areas from Indian River County north to Volusia County could see an additional 4 to 8 inches of rain through Friday night, with totals potentially topping 15 inches near the coast.
Reporter covering issues in national K-12 education
Proposed change to SNAP threatens free school meals for 1.7 million children

The Trump administration’s changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, cut more than 5 million people off from federal food benefits and eliminated free school meals for some students.
Now, a newly proposed rule threatens free school meals for nearly 2 million children.

The Agriculture Department wants to limit a provision called “broad-based categorical eligibility,” which allows families that receive certain public benefits to automatically qualify for SNAP, commonly known as food stamps.

The department, which runs SNAP, estimates the change could drop 6.3 million people from the food assistance program because they exceed income limits. Because SNAP recipients are automatically eligible for free school meals, the families of more than 1.7 million children affected by the change would have to fill out paperwork to apply for the free meals — or lose access to them.

Most of those children — 1.66 million — would still be living in households that qualify for free meals, according to USDA. School districts have said automatic enrollment has been helpful because many families don’t complete the paperwork. Districts end up footing the bill for those children’s meals.
USDA said the rule change would ensure SNAP can be accessed only by the households that need it most. Nutrition advocates argue it would exacerbate food insecurity.
The public can comment on the proposal until Dec. 10. If adopted, the rule will take effect in fall 2028.
Reporter covering breaking news from London
Van Gogh painting nets record $190.4M after dispute over its history

A Vincent van Gogh painting fetched a record-breaking $190.4 million at auction after a last-minute agreement between the sellers and the heirs of the painting’s former Jewish owners allowed the sale to proceed.
“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) went under the hammer at Sotheby’s on Wednesday evening, and secured the highest price ever paid for a Van Gogh artwork.
The 1890 painting “dates from the extraordinary period of creative intensity that marked the final two months of the artist’s life,” the auction house said.
The sale appeared uncertain last week, as descendants of the painting’s former owners, Samuel and Hedwig Fischer, said the family sold the painting in the 1930s due to Nazi persecution.

On the day of the auction, Sotheby’s confirmed that a deal between the Fischer heirs and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned the painting for more than 50 years, would allow the sale to proceed. “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history … the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution,” Sotheby’s said in a statement.
Gunnar Schnabel, an attorney for the Fischer heirs, said the family hopes the resolution “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era.”
